# .NET-derived JSON fixtures

`dotnet/*.json` is generated by [the linked-model oracle](../dotnet/README.md).
Keep these generated files in version control; consumers do not need .NET.

| File | Root / purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ping-info.json` | Array of real `PingInfo` serializations, including exact ulong IDs, uint dates, nullable ushort response times, and escaped text |
| `remove-ping-info.json` | Array of real `RemovePingInfo` serializations with the same ID boundaries |
| `swap-monitor-ping-info.json` | Array of real `SwapMonitorPingInfo` serializations (signed int ID) |
| `ping-params.json` | Array of real `PingParams` serializations |
| `alert-flag-obj.json` | Array of real `AlertFlagObj` serializations |
| `readiness-state.json` | Array of real `ReadinessState` serializations |
| `deserialization-cases.json` | Array of named inputs and observed .NET outcomes |
| `manifest.json` | Provenance, serializer profile, and file inventory |

Each deserialization case has `Name`, `Model`, `Input` (a JSON **string containing
the exact input document**), `Accepted`, `Normalized`, `Exception`, and
`ExceptionPath`. Decode the outer string and feed its contents to the parser
under test. Accepted cases contain the resulting serialized model in
`Normalized`; rejected cases contain null there and `JsonException` metadata.
An accepted root `null` also has `Normalized: null`, so distinguish outcomes by
`Accepted`. Exception paths are diagnostic, not a required C error message.

Numeric ID coverage includes 0, 1, 2147483647, 2147483648, 2147483649,
4294967295, 9007199254740992, 9007199254740993, and 18446744073709551615.
Do not decode these through `double`, signed 64-bit storage, or JavaScript
`Number`. Use exact unsigned integers or preserve numeric tokens. The fixtures
deliberately distinguish adjacent integers above the binary64 precision limit.

`DateSentInt` covers 0, 1, the signed-32 boundary and uint maximum. Nullable
`RoundTripTime` covers null, 0, 1, 65534 and 65535. Other cases cover overflow,
negative unsigned values, quoted numbers, fractional/exponent integer tokens,
wrong JSON kinds, nullability, missing fields, unknown/case-mismatched fields,
duplicate properties, comments, trailing commas, and property setter order.

Important real-model behavior: `[NotMapped]` affects database mapping, not
System.Text.Json. `PingInfo.DateSent`, `Status`, and `RoundTripTimeInt` remain in
JSON. `DateSent` and `DateSentInt` write the same backing value, so the last one
in an input object wins. Missing fields retain CLR/constructor defaults. A
non-nullable C# reference annotation does not by itself reject explicit JSON
null with this serializer profile (`SwapMonitorPingInfo.AppID` demonstrates it).

Compare C output structurally with exact numeric values and decoded strings;
whitespace, equivalent string escapes and object key ordering need not match.
Do preserve input property order when testing the setter-order probes. These
fixtures define observed .NET behavior, not extra domain validation. A C
consumer with intentionally different validation should document the difference.
